title: The Dal Khalsa, 1748
hook: at a Sarbat Khalsa in Amritsar the bands united into one army under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia

segments.voice: Yesterday, rakhi: Sikh bands guarding villages from plunder for a share of the harvest. Your line was keep the village safe. Who did you look out for? Today, the bands themselves face a choice. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

Horsemen are riding into Amritsar from every direction. Each group has its own leader, its own banner, its own story of the hard years. Some leaders have never ridden together. Some have quarreled. Each band has kept itself alive by being quick and independent, answering to no one but its own chief. Now they are all dismounting at the same place, near the Harmandir, for a gathering Sikhs call the Sarbat Khalsa: the whole Khalsa, together. On the table is a question that asks a lot of proud people. Should each of us keep riding alone? Today's word is the answer they gave: Dal Khalsa.
screen: `BANDS RIDE IN FROM EVERY SIDE.` → `EACH WITH ITS OWN CHIEF.` → `SARBAT KHALSA: THE WHOLE KHALSA.`

segments.voice: Dal means an army, a host. Dal Khalsa: the army of the Khalsa. This path met the name once before, alongside the gurmata, the decision the gathering makes together. Today, look at what the decision cost. Tradition says it was Nawab Kapur Singh, the humble leader who had once been fanning the sangat, who pressed for it. The scattered bands would become one army. They wouldn't disappear. Each chief kept his own band, his own riders. But they would answer to one command, and gather again at Amritsar to decide things together. And as the head of that one army, the gathering chose Jassa Singh Ahluwalia. So every chief in that gathering gave something up. Not his men, not his name, but the right to do whatever he liked. That's the hard part of unity. It's easy to agree that we'd be stronger together. It's much harder to be the one who steps back so it can happen. Where did the Sikhs get the nerve to try? From something older than the army. Guru Gobind Singh had founded the Khalsa as one body, with one initiation, drinking from one bowl. And the Sikh scripture speaks again and again of the sangat, the company of the faithful, as the place where the Guru is found. The Dal Khalsa took that spiritual idea and gave it saddles. There's something else worth noticing. The gathering decided in front of the Harmandir, with the Granth present. Sikhs understand those decisions as made in the Guru's presence, not just as a vote of the strongest. When the bands rode out of Amritsar, they rode out as one army.
screen: `DAL: AN ARMY, A HOST.` · `EACH CHIEF STEPPED BACK A LITTLE.` · `UNITY IS EASY TO PRAISE, HARD TO DO.` · `DECIDED IN THE GURU'S PRESENCE.` · then, large: `ONE ARMY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: join with others. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a group you belong to: a family, a team, a congregation, a group chat that's gone quiet. Notice where you've been riding alone in it, doing things your own way and waiting for the others to catch up. Ask honestly: what would I have to give up, a little, for this group to move together? An opinion held too tight, a habit, the need to be in charge. Don't decide anything yet. Just let yourself see it, and breathe with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and hold the group in mind. The bell holds the time.
Dal Khalsa. The army of the Khalsa: tradition says the scattered Sikh bands joined it at a Sarbat Khalsa in Amritsar, under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia. Today's word.
Your line: one army. Today, in one group you're part of, step back a little so the whole can move together. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs still speak of the Sarbat Khalsa, a gathering of the whole community at Amritsar, as the place where the Panth decides together in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib.

fork.setup: you're a chief of your own Sikh band. your riders have survived the hard years by being fast and answering to no one. at the Sarbat Khalsa, they propose one army. what do you do?
options: keep riding alone: independence kept you alive.
join, keep your band, and answer to one command.
join only if you're made the commander.
fork.reveal: tradition says the bands joined as one army under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia. each chief kept his men but gave up doing whatever he liked.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Dal Khalsa, the army of the Khalsa; dal means an army or host.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Dal Khalsa was just a big army.
what it means: it was the scattered Sikh bands choosing to answer to one command, each chief stepping back a little.
what a scholar hears: the bands kept their own chiefs inside the one army, and decisions were made together at Amritsar in the Guru's presence.

notes: Index title gives 1748; the script does not add a festival (often said to be Vaisakhi) or a count of bands (often eleven or twelve). Confirm.
Nawab Kapur Singh's role in proposing the union and Jassa Singh Ahluwalia's appointment as supreme commander: confirm the telling.
Year one (day 289) covered the Dal Khalsa and gurmata; this day takes the angle of what each chief gave up. Confirm no conflict.
'Dal means an army, a host': standard meaning, not an etymology claim; confirm.
'The Sikh scripture speaks again and again of the sangat' is a general description; confirm wording.
Audit pass: read in full; no changes. Dal Khalsa at Vaisakhi 1748 with Jassa Singh Ahluwalia at Nawab Kapur Singh's suggestion matches the standard telling.
